fault_protection_L1_001.notes: The ground_truth is well-supported by multiple retrieved engineering sources. All four shunt fault types (SLG, LL, LLG, 3P), their frequency ranking (SLG ~70-80% > LL ~15% > LLG ~10% > 3P ~2-5%), and the three-phase fault as most severe in terms of fault current are consistently confirmed. The candidate sources listed in the task file (IEEE Std 1547-2018, IEEE Std C37.112, Brearley & Prabu 2017 microgrid review) are not appropriate sources for this content — they cover DER interconnection, relay characteristics, and microgrid protection respectively, not shunt fault taxonomy or statistics. The real authoritative sources are standard power systems analysis textbooks (Glover/Sarma/Overbye, Bergen/Vittal) and the Westinghouse T&D Reference Book, though these were not directly fetchable. Multiple open-access web sources (all retrieved and confirmed) carry the same well-established engineering content. This is standard L1 power-engineering knowledge with no apparent question contamination.

fault_protection_L1_004.notes: The verbatim question text ("Describe four ways that high penetration of distributed energy resources (DERs) can disrupt conventional distribution protection that was designed for a radial, one-way power flow") does not appear as an exact match in any web source — contamination signal is 'not_found'. The Scielo open-access article (Shah et al. 2023) is the strongest source: it contains verbatim text covering all four mechanisms and explicitly states \"inverter-based DG limits the fault current around 2 times higher compared to the rated current,\" which aligns closely with the ground-truth claim of ~1.1–2x rated. The PMC article (Heliyon 2022) provides an independent open-access confirmation of the same phenomena. Most PDF sources were binary-encoded and could not be text-extracted by WebFetch. Many ResearchGate and MDPI pages returned 403. The LinkedIn practitioner article corroborates the terminology but is not peer-reviewed. Confidence is 0.82 because the Scielo source quotes the inverter limit as ~2x (not the 1.1–2x range stated in the ground truth), but is directionally consistent; the synchronous-vs-inverter distinction in fault current contribution is confirmed by multiple sources.

fault_protection_L1_005.notes: Two sources were successfully fetched and provide verbatim text supporting the ground-truth answer. Both confirm: (1) passive methods monitor local parameters (voltage, frequency) without perturbation — examples include ROCOF and OUV/OUF; (2) active methods inject disturbances — examples include Sandia Frequency Shift (SFS) and Slip-mode Frequency Shift (SMS); (3) NDZ is the range of conditions where detection fails; (4) passive methods are most vulnerable to NDZ and cannot reduce it to zero. Communication-based methods (zero NDZ) appear in search results but neither fetched page covers them in depth — the MDPI and ScienceDirect papers that explicitly discuss communication-based methods returned HTTP 403. Status is candidate_unverified rather than verified because: the fetched pages do not explicitly enumerate all three categories (passive/active/communication-based) in a single passage, and they do not use the exact phrasing of the ground truth. The contamination search found no verbatim match of the benchmark question text online.
